subject: ela
intro: When you share a story or describe something, a drawing or visual display can help your listener understand what you mean. A visual is helpful when words alone might leave the listener confused, or when showing something is faster and clearer than saying it. A good visual is directly connected to what you are describing — it shows something the listener could not picture from words alone. Not every visual helps. A picture that is not related to the content can confuse or distract the listener. When choosing a visual, ask: Does this show something my words cannot fully describe? Will my listener understand the content better after seeing this?

items.prompt:
A student is telling the class about butterflies. She says: 'A butterfly goes through four stages in its life. First it is an egg. Then it hatches into a caterpillar. Then it forms a chrysalis. Finally it becomes a butterfly.'

She is thinking about adding a visual. She has two options:
  Option A: A photograph of a garden with butterflies flying.
  Option B: A diagram showing the four stages of the butterfly life cycle in order, with labels.

Which visual is better? Why?

steps: The description is about a process: four stages in a specific order.
Option A (garden photo) shows butterflies but does not show the four stages or their order.
Option B (diagram with labels) directly shows the four stages in sequence, matching what the speaker is describing.
A good visual adds information the words cannot fully carry, or makes the sequence clearer.
The diagram helps a listener follow along — they can see each stage as the speaker names it.
solution.answer: Option B is better. The student is describing a sequence of four stages, and the diagram shows exactly that — in order, with labels. Option A shows butterflies but does nothing to help the listener understand the full life cycle. The best visual directly matches what is being described.

items.prompt:
A student is recounting a trip to his neighborhood. He says: 'My neighborhood has a park, a library, and a corner grocery store. To get from the park to the library, you walk two blocks north and then turn left. The grocery store is right across the street from the library.'

He is thinking about adding a visual. He has two options:
  Option A: A photograph of the inside of the library.
  Option B: A simple hand-drawn map showing the park, library, and grocery store with arrows.

Which visual is better? Why?

steps: The student is describing the layout of his neighborhood and how to get from one place to another.
Option A (inside of the library) shows one location but does not show the relationships between the three places.
Option B (a map) shows the relative positions of all three places and the direction of travel.
A map helps a listener understand spatial relationships that words can only partially convey.
The student is describing location and direction — a map is the ideal visual.
solution.answer: Option B is better. The student is describing where things are in relation to each other. A map shows that clearly. A photograph of the library's interior shows the listener what one place looks like, but it does not help them understand the neighborhood layout or directions. The best visual answers the question the description is trying to answer.

items.prompt:
A student is recounting the story of planting a garden with her grandmother. She says: 'We planted tomatoes, peppers, and sunflowers. My grandmother said to put the tomatoes on the south side because they need the most sun. We made rows and I used a stick to poke the holes for the seeds.'

She is thinking about adding a visual. She has two options:
  Option A: A drawing of the garden showing where each plant was placed, labeled with the plant names.
  Option B: A photograph of a supermarket vegetable aisle.

Which visual is better? Why?

steps: The student is describing the layout of the garden and where specific plants went.
Option A (drawing of the garden) shows exactly what is described: where each plant went and its label.
Option B (supermarket vegetable aisle) shows vegetables in a store, which is not connected to planting a garden.
Option B would confuse the listener — it does not match anything in the description.
Option A directly supports the description and helps the listener visualize the garden layout.
solution.answer: Option A is better. The student is describing where the plants went in the garden. A labeled drawing of the garden layout helps listeners picture exactly that. A supermarket photo is completely off-topic — it shows vegetables being sold, not planted. A visual must match what is being described.

items.prompt:
A student is describing what a spider web looks like. She says: 'Spider webs are made of very thin silk threads. The silk goes out from the center like bicycle spokes, and then more threads spiral around in circles. The circles get bigger as they get farther from the center.'

She is thinking about adding a visual. She has two options:
  Option A: A close-up photograph of a spider web with dew drops, showing the spoke-and-spiral pattern clearly.
  Option B: A photograph of a spider.

Which visual is better? Why?

steps: The student is describing the structure of a spider web: spokes and spirals.
Option A (close-up of the web) shows the structure she is describing, including both the spokes and the spiraling circles.
Option B (photograph of a spider) shows the animal but not the structure of the web.
The student is talking about the web, not the spider, so the spider photo is off-topic.
Option A directly matches the description and helps listeners see what spoke-and-spiral means.
solution.answer: Option A is better. The student is explaining the structure of a web — spokes and spirals. A close-up photograph of the web lets listeners see exactly what those patterns look like. A photograph of a spider does not help at all with understanding web structure. Choose a visual that shows what the words are describing.

items.prompt:
A student is recounting a hike he took with his family. He says: 'We hiked the Blue Ridge Trail, which goes up a steep hill and then flattens out near a waterfall. The whole trail is about three miles. On the way up, we passed two big boulders and a small stream you have to jump over.'

He is thinking about adding a visual. He has two options:
  Option A: A trail map showing the Blue Ridge Trail, the elevation, the two boulders, the stream, and the waterfall.
  Option B: A photograph of a waterfall.

Which visual is better? Why?

steps: The student is describing the layout and features of a trail: steep section, flat area, specific landmarks.
Option A (trail map) shows all of these: the shape of the trail, the elevation change, the boulders, the stream, and the waterfall.
Option B (waterfall photo) shows only one feature of the hike.
The student's description covers the whole trail, so the visual should too.
Option A allows listeners to follow the whole journey on the map as the student describes it.
solution.answer: Option A is better. The student is describing the full trail: its shape, length, elevation, and landmarks. A trail map shows all of those things in one image. A photograph of a waterfall shows only the endpoint and none of what happened along the way. When a description covers multiple features or a journey, a map or diagram is almost always the best visual.

items.prompt:
A student is describing his favorite book. He says: 'My favorite book is about a boy who builds a rocket ship in his backyard. He draws blueprints, collects parts from a junkyard, and takes three months to build it. In the end, the rocket actually works and he goes to the moon.'

He wants to add a visual. Here are two options:
  Option A: A drawing of the boy's blueprints for the rocket, showing the labeled parts.
  Option B: A photograph of a real NASA rocket on a launchpad.

Which visual is better? Explain why.
items.hint: Think about which visual is directly connected to what the student described about this specific book.

steps: The student is describing a fictional book about a boy who builds a rocket from blueprints and junkyard parts.
Option A (blueprints drawing) matches the story directly — blueprints are mentioned in the description.
Option B (NASA rocket) is real-world information about an actual rocket, not related to this fictional story.
The visual should support the specific description, not just the general topic.
Option A helps listeners understand the boy's project; Option B is a different rocket entirely.
solution.answer: Option A is better. The description specifically mentions blueprints, so a drawing of those blueprints is directly connected to what the student described. A photograph of a real NASA rocket is about space exploration, not this fictional story. A good visual matches the specific content of the description, not just the general subject.

items.prompt:
A student is describing how volcanoes erupt. She says: 'When a volcano erupts, hot melted rock called magma pushes up from underground. When magma reaches the surface, we call it lava. The lava flows down the sides of the volcano and can travel very far before it cools and hardens.'

She wants to add a visual. Here are two options:
  Option A: A diagram showing a cross-section of a volcano, with arrows pointing from the underground magma, up through the opening, and out as lava flowing down the side.
  Option B: A photograph of a mountain covered in snow.

Which visual is better? Explain why.
items.hint: The student is describing something happening inside and outside the volcano. Which visual shows both?

steps: The student is describing a process: magma underground, eruption, lava flowing down the side.
Option A (cross-section diagram) shows the inside and outside of the volcano, with the flow of magma to lava.
Option B (snow-covered mountain) is a mountain, not a volcano, and shows nothing about eruption.
A diagram with arrows can show a process — exactly what the student is describing.
Option A directly matches the description; Option B is off-topic.
solution.answer: Option A is better. The student is describing a process that happens both inside and outside the volcano. A cross-section diagram with arrows shows exactly that process — magma underground becoming lava on the surface. A photograph of a snowy mountain does not show a volcano or an eruption and would confuse the listener.

items.prompt:
A student is recounting the story of her family's first day in a new city. She says: 'When we arrived, we did not speak much English. My mom held a piece of paper with our new address written on it. We took the subway for the first time, and a woman sitting across from us pointed us to the right stop without saying a word — she just smiled and pointed.'

She wants to add a visual to share alongside this story. Here are two options:
  Option A: A photograph of a crowded city street.
  Option B: A drawing of the subway map showing their route, with the starting stop and the destination stop circled.

Which visual is better? Explain why.
items.hint: The student's story centers on a specific journey on the subway. Which visual shows that journey?

steps: The student is recounting a specific subway journey: a starting point and a destination they had to find.
Option B (subway map with the route circled) shows exactly what happened: where they started and where they needed to go.
Option A (city street photo) shows a generic city scene — it is not connected to the subway journey.
The map helps listeners understand the disorientation of navigating an unfamiliar subway for the first time.
Option B directly supports the story; Option A does not.
solution.answer: Option B is better. The student's story is about navigating the subway for the first time in a new city. A subway map with the route circled shows exactly the journey she described — where they started, where they needed to go, and the uncertainty of getting there. A city street photograph does not show any of that. The best visual makes the story easier to follow.

items.prompt:
A student is describing what a coral reef looks like. He says: 'A coral reef is full of colorful coral of all different shapes. Some coral looks like fans, some looks like brain ridges, and some grows in tall stacks. Many fish swim between the different types of coral.'

He wants to add a visual. Here are two options:
  Option A: An underwater photograph of a coral reef showing fan coral, brain coral, and stacked coral with fish swimming through.
  Option B: A photograph of the ocean from a boat.

Which visual is better? Explain why.
items.hint: The student is describing specific shapes inside the reef. Which visual shows those shapes?

steps: The student is describing specific types and shapes of coral inside a reef.
Option A (underwater photo of a reef) shows the fan coral, brain coral, and stacked coral he described — with fish swimming through.
Option B (ocean from a boat) shows the surface of the water — nothing of the reef or coral at all.
Option A is directly connected to every detail in the description.
Option B would give the listener no new understanding of what a coral reef looks like.
solution.answer: Option A is better. The student described specific types of coral with specific shapes. An underwater photograph showing those types of coral lets the listener see exactly what he is talking about. A photograph of the ocean surface shows nothing of what is inside the reef. A visual should show what the words are describing, not just something vaguely related.

items.prompt:
A student is recounting a time when her class measured the height of sunflowers they had been growing. She says: 'We measured our sunflowers every week for six weeks. At first they were only two inches tall. By week three they were a foot tall. By week six they were almost five feet tall. We recorded the measurements on a chart.'

She wants to share a visual with the class. Here are two options:
  Option A: The actual bar chart showing the sunflower's height each week from week one to week six.
  Option B: A photograph of sunflowers at a garden store.

Which visual is better? Explain why.
items.hint: The student is describing growth over time with numbers. Which visual shows that data?

steps: The student is describing growth over time: six weeks, increasing heights from 2 inches to almost 5 feet.
Option A (bar chart from the class) shows exactly that data — each week's measurement, so the listener can see the growth.
Option B (garden store photo) shows sunflowers but not the growth data being described.
The student even mentions they recorded measurements on a chart — Option A is that chart.
Option A directly supports every number in the description; Option B is decorative only.
solution.answer: Option A is better. The student's description is entirely about numbers: how tall the sunflowers were each week over six weeks. The bar chart shows exactly that information in a way the listener can see and understand. A photograph of sunflowers at a garden store does not show any of the data. When a description is about numbers or change over time, a chart or graph is the ideal visual.
